title.zh: 旧金山迷幻之重要乐队

summary.en: The Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, Janis Joplin, and Country Joe and the Fish were among the important musicians of the San Francisco psychedelic scene.
summary.zh: The Grateful Dead、The Jefferson Airplane、Janis Joplin和Country Joe and the Fish等都是旧金山迷幻场景中的重要音乐人。

body.zh:
The Grateful Dead、The Jefferson Airplane、Janis Joplin和Country Joe and the Fish等都是旧金山迷幻场景中的重要音乐人。

我们现在转向旧金山的音乐人、亚文化及一些重要乐队。当然，你可能已经知道我要谈的一些艺术家：The Grateful Dead, The Jefferson Airplane, Janis Joplin，还会聊聊Country Joe and the Fish。让我们先谈谈这些音乐人为何属于迷幻场景，以及什么样的音乐才称得上迷幻。

The Grateful Dead于 1965 年成立，一开始叫做The Warlocks，他们演奏滚石乐队的歌曲和芝加哥电声布鲁斯（Chicago Electric Blues）。他们的根源是美国传统民谣和jug band music（水罐乐队音乐）。（注：jug band是使用水罐和传统自制乐器演奏的乐队。这些自制乐器是为发出声音而改装的普通物品，如搓衣板、勺子、骨头、梳子和纸等。）那时Jerry Garcia、Phil Lesh和Bob Weir已经在乐队中了，他们中的一些人开始为Ken Kesey进行迷幻测试。随着场景开始在旧金山发展，他们也开始了演奏。天哪，当你查看旧金山各种活动的海报时，很难找到一张没有The Grateful Dead的，他们一直在演出。他们发明了一种高度即兴的方法，正如Jerry Garcia过去常说的那样：不管我们尝试演奏什么曲子，不管它的原始版本有多短，我们开始演奏，然后它慢慢变长。因为他们喜欢做的不是完全自由式的即兴创作，虽然有时他们会这样做，但他们只是喜欢把曲调拉长，创造这种拉长版自由式即兴音乐。周围是使用迷幻药物的人群和五彩缤纷的灯光，人们不像在Dick Clark的American Bandstand节目上那样跳舞，而是以各种方式做自由式舞蹈。这真的很适合The Grateful Dead正在演奏的歌曲。

我们需要意识到，关于The Grateful Dead的一个重要事情是，由于这种即兴，他们主要是一支现场乐队。你想听他们的现场演奏，同一首歌听多少遍都没关系，因为每一次都不一样。他们没有将一首歌的一个特定版本固定到一张专辑中，并拥有一个权威版本，这对The Grateful Dead来说是陌生的。例如，你想到《Sgt. Pepper》那些曲调，它们的录制方式，他们在录音室里所做的一切，就是那样子。再比如，The Beach Boys的《Pet Sounds》必须是那样，对吧？ 因此，如果你听The Beatles或者致敬乐队的表演，你会希望他们按照唱片上的方式演奏。但是对The Grateful Dead来说，并非如此。

所以多年来The Grateful Dead在唱片上表现一般，尽管他们在1967年3月录制了一张名为《The Grateful Dead》的专辑，但大多数乐迷会说这不是好的代表作。1968年的《Anthem of The Sun》也不是好的代表做，但是歌曲《That's It For The Other One》是由Jerry Garcia和Phil Lesh在录音室里用之前完成的各种现场表演的录音带拼接而成的，以一种随机的方式淡入和淡出各段表演。这听起来非常先锋，如果你用恰当的方式剪辑后播放给音乐学校的学生，告诉他们这是以前从未听过的Karlheinz Stockhausen（注：德国作曲家，音乐理论家，音乐教育家）的作品，他们肯定会相信。他们会非常惊讶这是The Grateful Dead的作品，非常实验，先锋，噪音，没有明确的和弦进行。很多即兴演奏就像1970年专辑《Live/Dead》里的《Dark Star》，使用将solo拉长等技法。The Grateful Dead雄心勃勃，非常了解现代和先锋音乐中发生的事情。Phil Lesh曾经学习过电子作曲，对此有所了解。当然他还参与了旧金山的磁带中心（tape center），是一个致力于电子音乐和科技的地方，这有点像The Grateful Dead玩的东西。这就是The Grateful Dead作为一支现场乐队主要做的事情。

相比起来，The Jefferson Airplane也有很多时髦的现场表演，很多即兴，但是他们也写出了很多单曲。The Grateful Dead并没有很多适合电台播放的单曲，而是让人们体验整个概念，但是The Jefferson Airplane在AM电台播放上却有不俗表现。他们最初由Marty Balin和Paul Kantner于1965年成立，在1966年做了专辑《Jefferson Airplane Takes Off》。但是直到Grace Slick以主唱身份加入后，乐队才真正起飞。她来自一个叫The Great Society的乐队，带来了几首曲目——《Somebody to Love》和《White Rabbit》都出自1967年专辑《Surrealistic Pillow》，都是AM电台热门单曲。1967年的美国，《Somebody to Love》获得了榜单第五，《White Rabbit》榜单第八。他们当然很乐意在现场演奏这些歌曲，但是节目中也有很多即兴表演。The Jefferson Airplane的武器库里有流行歌曲，The Grateful Dead没有，但这并没有困扰到他们。

另一个有热门歌曲创作潜力的艺术家是Janis Joplin。她出生在得克萨斯州的Port Arthur，然后去到旧金山，以Big Brother and the Holding Company乐队成员的身份出道。像The Grateful Dead一样，Big Brother and the Holding Company现场会做很多疯狂的事情。例如，他们有自己版本的《Hall of the Mountain King》，这首歌来自Grieg的《Peer Gynt》，是著名的古典音乐。（注：《Peer Gynt》是挪威著名剧作家易卜生的代表作之一，由Edvard Hagerup Grieg为其撰写配乐。）他们还有首歌叫《Bacon》，在某种意义上很像John Cage。这件作品的前提是，有人会在舞台上拿一个便携式炉子和煎锅，放几片培根（Bacon）在里面，然后乐队开始即兴，培根熟了歌曲就结束，歌曲长度跟做熟培根的时间一样长。尽管Janis Joplin有出自Big Brother and the Holding Company的热门单曲，也是个独立艺人，但是要知道这种即兴先锋风格在旧金山的迷幻场景中其实非常普遍。Janis在Big Brother and the Holding Company时期的最佳专辑当属1968年发行的《Cheap Thrills》，位列榜单第一。专辑是在旧金山的Fillmore录音室录制的，你可以感受到彼时正在发生的事情。其中歌曲《Piece of my Heart》相信你听过很多次，是FM摇滚电台的常驻曲目。一个趣事是，Janis翻唱了George Gershwin的《Summertime》，你或许想问，为什么要翻唱《Summertime》呢？但是你知道他们都翻唱过古典歌曲，所以为什么不呢？《Summertime》当然是一首美妙的歌曲，她也唱得很好。她翻唱Big Mama Thornton的《Ball and Chain》，证明了她真的很擅长演唱布鲁斯，这是一种天赋。她也许是60年代最好的布鲁斯歌手之一，至少是最好的女歌手。

不管怎样，她离开了乐队，开启了个人演艺生涯。她的最佳专辑大概是《Pearl》，于1971年初登上榜单第一，其中包括同为榜单第一的热门歌曲《Me and Bobby McGee》，由Kris Kristofferson创作。但成功是苦乐参半的，因为发生在去世后。事实上，Janis Joplin于1970年10月4日死于药物使用过量。所以《Pearl》是在死后发行的，并与单曲《Me and Bobby McGee》一起登上了第一名。

目前为止，本课程中我们谈及了许多女性艺术家，有女子组合（girl groups）、Jefferson Airplane的Grace Slick、Janis Joplin等等，但是他们都是摇滚乐中的白人女性。当我们谈论非裔美国艺术家时，那些大多数都是黑人。因此，我认为牢记这一点很重要：当我们在摇滚乐的历史中前行时，情况确实会发生改变。女性有了更多的控制地位，而不只是亮点，我们会在之后的课程中讲到。现在，我们把Grace Slick和Janis Joplin等人标记为早期人物。

我们要说的最后一支乐队是Country Joe and the Fish。当谈论旧金山时，要注意旧金山周围有两种场景。一种是旧金山嬉皮士，他们大多是非政治性的，不想卷入政治事件。他们只希望政府不要管他们，这样就可以享受致幻药物带来的“神游”，他们并没有刻意参与政治。从某种意义上说，有点像乌托邦。这些人让加州大学伯克利分校周围的另一群人感到非常沮丧，他们通常被认为是伯克利激进分子，他们希望看到这个国家真正的政治变革。所以来自伯克利激进分子对政治和社会变革的强大推动力，与旧金山嬉皮士的那种不理不睬的玩乐态度逐渐融为了一体。但实际上，它们是非常不同的社区，彼此之间有一定程度的敌意。

在他们之间架起桥梁的一个乐队是Country Joe and the Fish，他们既创作嬉皮音乐，也创作与社会变革相关的音乐。在嬉皮方面，1967 年的专辑《Electric Music for the Mind and Body》，据乐队主唱Joe MacDonald所说，是为了伴随LSD神游而写的。专辑中所做的一切都是为了成为一种伴随LSD之旅的配乐，专辑完成后，他们服用了LSD，看看它效果如何。 在政治方面，一首叫做《I-Feel-Like-I'm-Fixin'-to-Die Rag》的歌曲你可能听过，是与越南战争有关的政治抗议歌曲，是反文化运动的一个重要组成部分。反文化运动不仅反对战争，还与当时的民权运动联手。（注：1960年代反文化运动（counterculture movement）是一种反文化反体制行为，这种现象首先发生在英国和美国，之后在1960年代初至70年代中期在西方世界大规模传播。伦敦、纽约和旧金山是早期反文化活动的温床。随着美国民权运动的演进，反文化运动获得了进一步发展，并随着美国政府对越南军事干预的扩大而演变为一场革命性的运动。）但同样，很多嬉皮士对这一切并没那么感兴趣，他们只是在寻找自己的个人高潮。Joe McDonald的另一首歌非常有名，叫做《The Fish Cheer》，他唱道“Give me an F, Give me a I, Give me an S, Give me an H.”组成Country Joe and the Fish的“Fish”。但在伍德斯托克，他把它改成了另一个以 F 开头的四字单词（FUCK），这个著名版本很多人听过，虽然该版本在收音机里的播放频率并不高。

当讨论即将结束时，我们要提一些其他旧金山乐队的名字，比如Moby Grape、Quicksilver Messenger Service和Steve Miller。当我们看待旧金山这几年的景象时，应该为之后的课程做一个心里记录，Santana是从旧金山场景中诞生的，从Santana中衍生出的Journey也是从该场景诞生的。当然Steve Miller在70年代比在60年代更成功。Sly and the Family Stone也诞生于旧金山场景。甚至那些谈论过的在60年代末取得成功的乐队，他们在70年代继续以其他乐队的身份发出旧金山的声音。

但正如我所说，在1967年之前，这些乐队中大多数只在旧金山亚文化中为人所知。当”爱之夏“运动（Summer of Love）发生时，全国媒体纷纷聚焦于此，突然间，旧金山的音乐被带到了全国各地，开始成为主流。The Grateful Dead、Moby Grape、Quicksilver Messenger Service和Steve Miller或许没那么火。但是像The Jefferson Airplane和Janis Joplin真的成了明星，从亚文化走向主流。以上就是旧金山发生的事情，在下节课中，我们会了解同时期伦敦的迷幻场景发生了什么。
body.en:
The Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, Janis Joplin, and Country Joe and the Fish were among the important musicians of the San Francisco psychedelic scene.

We turn now to San Francisco’s musicians, subculture, and key bands. You may already know some of the artists I will discuss: the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, Janis Joplin, and also Country Joe and the Fish. First: why these musicians belong to the psychedelic scene, and what music counts as psychedelic.

The Grateful Dead formed in 1965, first as the Warlocks, playing Rolling Stones songs and Chicago electric blues. Their roots were American traditional folk and jug-band music. (Note: a jug band uses jugs and homemade instruments—ordinary objects adapted for sound: washboard, spoons, bones, comb and paper, etc.) Jerry Garcia, Phil Lesh, and Bob Weir were already in the band; some of them began doing Acid Tests for Ken Kesey. As the San Francisco scene grew, they played. Look at posters for San Francisco events and it is hard to find one without the Grateful Dead—they were always on. They invented a highly improvisational method. As Jerry Garcia used to say: whatever tune we try to play, however short the original, we start and it slowly gets longer. Not always totally free improvisation—though sometimes they did that—but they liked stretching tunes into long freeform pieces. Around them, people on psychedelics under colorful lights did not dance as on Dick Clark’s American Bandstand; they danced freeform in all kinds of ways. That fit what the Grateful Dead were playing.

An important fact: because of that improvisation, they were mainly a live band. You want to hear them live; hearing the same song many times is fine, because each time is different. Fixing one authoritative album version of a song was foreign to them. Think of how Sgt. Pepper’s tunes were recorded—everything done that way in the studio. Or Pet Sounds: it has to be that way, right? So if you hear the Beatles or a tribute band, you want them to play as on the record. Not so for the Grateful Dead.

For years their records were only so-so. They cut a March 1967 album called The Grateful Dead; most fans say it is not a good representation. 1968’s Anthem of the Sun is not either—but “That’s It for the Other One” was built by Jerry Garcia and Phil Lesh in the studio by splicing earlier live tapes, fading sections in and out almost at random. It sounds very avant-garde; if you edit it the right way and play it for music students as unknown Stockhausen, they would believe it. They would be shocked it was the Grateful Dead—experimental, avant-garde, noisy, no clear chord progression. Much improvisation is like “Dark Star” on 1970’s Live/Dead, stretching solos and so on. The Grateful Dead were ambitious and well aware of modern and avant-garde music. Phil Lesh had studied electronic composition and knew that world; he was also involved with San Francisco’s tape center, dedicated to electronic music and technology—close to what the Dead did. That is mainly what they did as a live band.

By contrast, Jefferson Airplane also had hip live shows and lots of improvisation, but they also wrote singles. The Grateful Dead did not have many radio-friendly singles; they offered a whole concept. Jefferson Airplane did well on AM. Marty Balin and Paul Kantner formed them in 1965; in 1966 they made Jefferson Airplane Takes Off. But they really took off after Grace Slick joined as singer. She came from the Great Society and brought songs—“Somebody to Love” and “White Rabbit,” both on 1967’s Surrealistic Pillow, both AM hits. In 1967 America, “Somebody to Love” hit No. 5 and “White Rabbit” No. 8. They were happy to play them live, but shows also had much improvisation. Jefferson Airplane had pop songs in the arsenal; the Grateful Dead did not—and that did not bother the Dead.

Another artist with hit potential was Janis Joplin. Born in Port Arthur, Texas, she went to San Francisco and debuted with Big Brother and the Holding Company. Like the Grateful Dead, Big Brother did wild things live. They had their own “Hall of the Mountain King,” from Grieg’s Peer Gynt—famous classical music. (Note: Peer Gynt is a major play by Norwegian dramatist Ibsen; Edvard Grieg wrote the score.) They also had a piece called “Bacon,” a bit like John Cage in spirit: someone brought a portable stove and frying pan onstage, put bacon in, and the band improvised until the bacon was done—song length equaled cooking time. Though Janis had hits with Big Brother and as a solo artist, know that this improvisational avant-garde style was very common in San Francisco psychedelia. Her best Big Brother album is 1968’s Cheap Thrills, No. 1. Recorded at Fillmore in San Francisco; you can feel what was happening. “Piece of My Heart” you have heard many times—an FM rock staple. A side note: she covered Gershwin’s “Summertime”—why? They all covered classical songs, so why not? It is a beautiful song and she sings it well. Covering Big Mama Thornton’s “Ball and Chain” showed she really could sing blues—a gift. She may have been one of the best blues singers of the 1960s, at least among women.

Anyway she left the band for a solo career. Her best album is probably Pearl, No. 1 in early 1971, with the No. 1 hit “Me and Bobby McGee” by Kris Kristofferson. Success was bittersweet—it came after her death. Janis Joplin died of a drug overdose on 4 October 1970. Pearl was released posthumously and, with that single, hit No. 1.

So far in this course we have mentioned many women artists—girl groups, Grace Slick of Jefferson Airplane, Janis Joplin, and so on—but they are white women in rock. When we talk African American artists, most of those figures are Black men. Keep that in mind: as we move through rock history, things do change. Women gain more control, not only as highlights; we will cover that later. For now mark Grace Slick and Janis Joplin as early figures.

Last band: Country Joe and the Fish. Around San Francisco, note two scenes. One is San Francisco hippies, mostly nonpolitical—they did not want politics. They wanted government to leave them alone so they could enjoy LSD trips; they did not deliberately enter politics. In a sense, a utopia. That frustrated another group around UC Berkeley, usually called Berkeley radicals, who wanted real political change. So the strong push for political and social change from Berkeley radicals gradually mixed with the San Francisco hippies’ leave-us-alone playfulness. In fact they were very different communities with some hostility.

One band bridging them was Country Joe and the Fish—hippie music and music tied to social change. On the hippie side, 1967’s Electric Music for the Mind and Body was, according to singer Joe McDonald, written to accompany an LSD trip. Everything on the album was meant as a soundtrack for the trip; when it was done they took LSD to see how it worked. On the political side, “I-Feel-Like-I’m-Fixin’-to-Die Rag”—you may know it—is a Vietnam War protest song, an important part of the counterculture. That movement opposed the war and also joined the civil-rights struggle. (Note: the 1960s counterculture was anti-establishment first in Britain and the U.S., then across the West from the early 1960s into the mid-1970s. London, New York, and San Francisco were early beds. As the civil-rights movement grew and U.S. intervention in Vietnam expanded, it became more revolutionary.) Many hippies, though, were not that interested; they sought their own highs. Another famous Joe McDonald song is “The Fish Cheer”: “Give me an F, Give me an I, Give me an S, Give me an H”—spelling Fish. At Woodstock he changed it to another four-letter F-word; that famous version many have heard, though radio did not play it much.

As we close, name other San Francisco bands: Moby Grape, Quicksilver Messenger Service, Steve Miller. Looking at these years, mark for later courses that Santana came out of this scene, and Journey from Santana’s orbit. Steve Miller was more successful in the 1970s than the 1960s. Sly and the Family Stone also came from San Francisco. Even bands that succeeded in the late 1960s kept putting out a San Francisco sound in the 1970s under other names.

But as I said, before 1967 most of these bands were known only in the San Francisco subculture. When the Summer of Love hit, national media focused there; suddenly San Francisco music went nationwide and into the mainstream. The Grateful Dead, Moby Grape, Quicksilver Messenger Service, and Steve Miller may not have been that huge. But Jefferson Airplane and Janis Joplin really became stars, from subculture to mainstream. That is what happened in San Francisco; next time, the London psychedelic scene in the same years.
